title: Isn't It Ironic, Dontcha Think?
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore irony as a concept: its origins in the Greek "eiron" stock character, Socratic irony, Quintilian's definition, the Romantics and Hegel/Kierkegaard's critiques, dramatic and situational irony (Oedipus Rex, Thurwall), verbal irony vs. sarcasm, litotes, cosmic irony (George Carlin's insulin/sugar bit), romantic irony, satire (Swift's A Modest Proposal), camp, O. Henry, The Monkey's Paw, M. Night Shyamalan, Fight Club, David Foster Wallace, the "Death of Irony" and Dave Eggers, and Gen Z meta irony. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about White Boy Rick's surname and the East Detroit naming confusion.

entities.name: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

segments.title: Intro and Alanis Morissette's 'Ironic'
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the irony episode and discuss Alanis Morissette's song 'Ironic' and whether its examples are truly ironic, plus Reality Bites and the difficulty of defining irony.

segments.title: Origins: eiron, Socratic irony, Quintilian, and the Renaissance
segments.summary: The term comes from the Greek 'eiron' stock character who plays dumb, as in Socratic irony. Quintilian defined it as saying something contrary to what you mean. Renaissance thinkers identified the irony of fate, now called situational irony.

segments.title: German Romantics, Hegel, and Kierkegaard
segments.summary: The German Romantics prized irony as a way to question conventional wisdom. Hegel disliked it as smart-alecky, and Kierkegaard called it infinite absolute negativity and linked it to loss of meaning.

segments.title: Dramatic irony and Oedipus Rex
segments.summary: Thirlwall applied the term dramatic irony in 1833, where the audience knows what characters do not. Oedipus Rex is discussed as an example of layered irony.

segments.title: Verbal irony, sarcasm, and litotes
segments.summary: Verbal irony is distinguished from sarcasm, which is seen as more vicious, and litotes is introduced as understated verbal irony.

segments.title: Situational irony, black comedy, and cosmic irony
segments.summary: Situational irony is discussed with examples like a lifeguard drowning and a fire station burning. Cosmic irony is introduced as karmic irony, and George Carlin's sugar versus insulin delivery truck distinction is recounted.

segments.title: Dramatic irony, romantic irony, and Broadcast News
segments.summary: Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example illustrates dramatic irony. Romantic irony, breaking the fourth wall, is discussed, along with Albert Brooks and Broadcast News.

segments.title: Philosophical irony and One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest
segments.summary: Philosophical irony is described as playing dumb, with McMurphy in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest offered as an example of a sane person in a mental hospital.
topics: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

segments.title: Satire and A Modest Proposal
segments.summary: Chuck proposes that satire may be harmful by releasing pressure for change. Josh offers the view that conversation is the point. Swift's A Modest Proposal (1729) is cited.

segments.title: Camp and John Waters
segments.summary: Camp is introduced as ironic appreciation, with John Waters' definition on The Simpsons.

segments.title: Break and recap of universal verbal irony
segments.summary: Break, then a recap that verbal irony appears universal and kindergarteners grasp it; a universal nickname example for a big person is mentioned.

segments.title: Literary irony: Zhuangzi, Tom Sawyer, Don Quixote, O. Henry, Monkey's Paw
segments.summary: Examples of ancient and literary irony: the twisted tree in Zhuangzi, Tom Sawyer's fence trick, Don Quixote, O. Henry's twists, and W.W. Jacobs' The Monkey's Paw.

segments.title: M. Night Shyamalan, Catch-22, and Fight Club
segments.summary: Hosts compare O. Henry to M. Night Shyamalan and discuss his films including The Village and Sixth Sense. Catch-22's paradox and Fight Club's irony are discussed.

segments.title: Chuck's view on satire and final thoughts on irony
segments.summary: Chuck explains his dislike of satire and says cosmic and situational irony are to be appreciated while human-created irony is often poorly done.

segments.title: David Foster Wallace, Death of Irony, Dave Eggers, and Gen Z meta irony
segments.summary: David Foster Wallace's critique of overused irony is discussed, followed by the Death of Irony backlash and Dave Eggers, and Gen Z's meta irony and absurdism.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the irony discussion, noting it is hard to define and talked about for nearly 48 minutes.

segments.title: Listener mail: White Boy Rick and East Detroit
segments.summary: Mike from East Point, Michigan corrects the pronunciation of Worsley and clarifies that the Curry Brothers were based on Detroit's east side, not the city of East Detroit, which renamed itself East Point.
